subject: Civil Engineering
title: Claims and Disputes
description: A micro-lesson that makes Claims and Disputes usable.

hook.text: The contractor says the delay was the owner's fault. The owner disagrees. A claim is born.

buildup.text: Construction claims arise from delays, differing site conditions, or scope changes.

discovery.text: Time-impact analysis reconstructs the schedule to prove who caused each day of delay.

twist.text: Disputes can exceed the original contract value — litigation lasts years and costs millions.

climax.text: Arbitration and mediation resolve most construction disputes — faster and cheaper than court.

punchline.text: Documentation wins disputes. The party with better records usually prevails.

quiz.question: What typically resolves construction disputes faster than litigation?
options: Ignoring the dispute until the project is complete
Arbitration and mediation — structured resolution processes outside of court
Hiring more lawyers to accelerate the court proceedings

details.summary: Construction claims are formal demands for additional compensation or time beyond the contract amount, arising when parties disagree on responsibility for cost overruns, delays, or scope changes.
details.whyItMatters: Claims and disputes consume enormous time, money, and management attention. Major disputes can bankrupt contractors and delay projects by years. Prevention is far more effective than resolution.
takeaways: Claims require contemporaneous documentation of events, costs, and impacts
Mediation resolves most disputes faster and cheaper than arbitration or litigation
Dispute review boards provide ongoing neutral evaluation during projects

faq.question: What documentation is needed to support a construction delay claim?
faq.answer: Effective delay claims require contemporaneous daily logs, photographs, correspondence, schedule updates showing critical path impact, weather records, and documentation of notice given per contract requirements.

faq.question: What is a Dispute Review Board and how does it work?
faq.answer: A DRB is a panel of three neutral experts appointed at project start who visit the site regularly, review progress, and provide non-binding recommendations when disputes arise. Their early involvement and project knowledge produces faster, more informed resolution.
